subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: "Last tray! Counter closes in five minutes!" the caterer shouted across the noisy wedding hall. Pradeep, five, ran to the kids' table, where a big steel tray of gulab jamun sat steaming. His cousin Chaitanya was already there, scooping with both hands. Pradeep piled four into his paper plate, then two more, fast, before they were gone. More children pushed in. In a minute the tray held only syrup. Little Guddi, three, arrived late and stared at it. Pradeep looked at his plate. Syrup was dripping through the paper onto his new shoes, and he couldn't eat even three.

qa.q: How many gulab jamun did Pradeep put in his plate altogether?
qa.a: Pradeep piled four into his paper plate, then two more, so six gulab jamun.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep grab so many so quickly?
qa.a: He was afraid the tray would be empty soon, because the caterer said it was the last tray and Chaitanya was already scooping with both hands.

qa.q: What could the grown-ups have done when the last tray came out?
qa.a: They could have handed out two each to the children in a line, so nobody had to rush and grab before it was gone.

qa.q: How might Guddi feel when she reaches the table and finds only syrup?
qa.a: Guddi might feel left out and sad, because the older children took everything before she even got there.

grounding: A five-year-old at a wedding grabs far more sweets than he can eat because others are grabbing, and the shared tray is emptied before a small child gets any.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: On Diwali evening Aparna Aunty from 3B put a steel bowl of coconut barfi on the stair landing. "For all the building children!" she called, and went back inside. Rukmini, four, heard feet thundering down the stairs. She ran too. Big hands were in the bowl. Rukmini grabbed five pieces and pushed them into her frock pocket. The bowl was empty before old Mr Joshi from the ground floor even reached the landing. Later, Rukmini put her hand in her pocket. The barfi had turned into warm, crumbly mush. She licked her fingers and looked at the empty bowl.

qa.q: Where did Aparna Aunty put the bowl of barfi?
qa.a: She put it on the stair landing on Diwali evening, for all the building children.

qa.q: What was going through Rukmini's mind when she heard feet thundering down the stairs?
qa.a: She was worried the barfi would all go to the bigger children, so she hurried and took five pieces before anyone else could take them.

qa.q: What small step could have kept the barfi for everyone?
qa.a: If each child had taken one piece and waited, there would have been enough for everyone, including Mr Joshi, and nothing would have turned to mush.

qa.q: How might Aparna Aunty feel if she came out and saw the empty bowl?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a bit disappointed that her treat for all the children was gone in a rush, with some people getting none.

grounding: A four-year-old stuffs her pocket with shared sweets because others are grabbing, and the bowl empties before everyone gets a share.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: The Class 5 paint tubs were bought with everyone's craft fund. On Monday Yamini, ten, squeezed out a huge blob of blue for a tiny sky, and left the lid off. "There's loads," she told Vaibhav. "My little bit won't finish it." Vaibhav squeezed out red the same way. So did the table behind them. Nobody put lids back, because nobody thought one open tub mattered. By Thursday the blue had a hard, cracked crust. The yellow was dry as chalk. When Ms Pinto announced the Independence Day posters, there was almost no paint left. Yamini poked the crust with her brush and said nothing.

qa.q: What did the paint tubs look like by Thursday?
qa.a: The blue had a hard, cracked crust and the yellow was dry as chalk.

qa.q: What did Yamini believe about her own use of the paint on Monday?
qa.a: She believed her little bit would not matter because there was loads of paint, so she did not bother with the lid.

qa.q: What could Yamini do differently with the next set of shared paints?
qa.a: She could squeeze out only what she needs and close the lid each time, and suggest the class does the same, since the paint belongs to everyone.

qa.q: How are the rest of the class affected when the posters are announced?
qa.a: Everyone, including children who were careful, now has almost no paint for the Independence Day posters, even though the craft fund was theirs too.

grounding: A ten-year-old wastes class paint thinking her share cannot matter, everyone does the same, and the shared paint is spoiled for all.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: "Nirmala! Why is there no water in the bathroom?" Mummy called. "The whole building's tank is empty." Nirmala, eleven, looked at her little brother Tenzin. Tenzin looked at the ceiling. "We were washing our cycles on the terrace," he said. "With the hose," Nirmala added. "Only for a bit." "How long is a bit?" "Maybe... an hour? The Mehtas' kids were also doing it. And the boys from the fourth floor were having a water fight." Mummy sat down. "So everyone thought their bit was small." "One hose can't empty a whole tank, Mummy." "Five hoses can." Tenzin whispered, "Mrs Rao can't cook now, can she?" Nirmala felt her face go hot. "We could carry her a bucket from the corner tap."

qa.q: What were Nirmala and Tenzin doing on the terrace?
qa.a: They were washing their cycles with the hose.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels guilty once Mummy points out the problem?
qa.a: Her face goes hot when Tenzin mentions Mrs Rao, and she quickly offers to carry a bucket to her.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene could change how the children use the terrace hose?
qa.a: The moment Mummy says five hoses can empty the tank shows them their bit was not small, so next time they could use a bucket and stop quickly.

qa.q: How are neighbours like Mrs Rao affected by what the children did?
qa.a: Mrs Rao cannot cook because the whole building's tank is empty, even though she had nothing to do with the hoses.

grounding: An eleven-year-old and other children each waste the building's shared water thinking one hose does not matter, and the tank runs dry for everyone.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: In the government school at Sironj, the Class 10 science project was to test water from four village hand pumps. Gopal, fifteen, was in the group of six. From the back bench he watched it happen week after week. Payal walked to the pumps with bottles after school. Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand. The other four, Gopal among them, said, "Tell us what to do," and then went to the tea stall. Nobody had a named job, so nobody felt it was theirs. On Friday Vandana slammed the file on the desk. "We are not your servants." Payal did not say anything, but she did not smile all day. Gopal saw it then: the careful ones had carried everything, and now they were fed up.

qa.q: Who wrote up every result for the project?
qa.a: Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand.

qa.q: What does Gopal realise on Friday?
qa.a: He sees that because nobody had a named job, the careful ones carried everything and are now fed up, and he realises he was one of those who went to the tea stall.

qa.q: What choice could Gopal make now that he has seen the problem?
qa.a: He could ask the group to give each person a named job, and take one of the pump visits or write-ups himself.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to feel by Friday, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seems quietly hurt and tired of carrying the work, because she stays silent and does not smile all day.

grounding: A teenage boy watches his group leave the project to two diligent girls and sees how having no named jobs leaves them carrying the load and resenting it.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: In their school in Porto Alegre, the science-fair team had five names on the sign-up sheet. Emil, sixteen, noticed who actually stayed after the bell. Priscila, every day, rewiring the little wind turbine. Tomás, cutting blades out of plastic bottles. The other three, Emil included, kept saying, "Message us if you need anything," and walked out. On Wednesday the turbine would not spin. Priscila stayed until the caretaker switched off the lights. The next morning Emil heard her tell Tomás, "If our names are on it, why is it only us?" Tomás only shrugged and rubbed his eyes, looking worn out. Emil thought about the sign-up sheet in his bag. Five names, but no one was down for any single job, so three of them could vanish and nobody would notice. Except those two.

qa.q: What were Priscila and Tomás making for the science fair?
qa.a: They were building a little wind turbine, with Priscila rewiring it and Tomás cutting blades out of plastic bottles.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she spoke to Tomás the next morning?
qa.a: She was frustrated and resentful, asking why only the two of them did the work when all five names were on the project.

qa.q: What could Emil do with what he has noticed?
qa.a: He could suggest writing one job next to each name on the sheet and take on a real part of the turbine himself instead of just offering to help by message.

qa.q: How does the situation look from Tomás's side?
qa.a: He is worn out from doing the work while others leave, and his tired shrug suggests he has stopped expecting the others to help.

grounding: A teenage boy observes that when no one has a named job, two careful teammates carry the whole project and grow resentful.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Week one. The student house in Melbourne had four rooms and one kitchen. Sahil, twenty, cooked dal on Monday and left the pot soaking. "I'll do it tomorrow," he told Dolma. She laughed. "My plate's in there too."

Week two. The pot was still there, under three frying pans, a tower of bowls and a colander nobody would own. Fruit flies hovered over the bin. Everyone ate toast in their rooms. Sahil walked past the sink each night thinking, one pot is nothing compared with all that.

Week three. Dolma pinned a list to the fridge: every dirty item and whose it was. Sahil read it slowly. The pot, two mugs, a pan, a fork. Each line was small. Together, his lines were a quarter of the mess.

qa.q: What did Dolma pin to the fridge in week three?
qa.a: She pinned a list of every dirty item and whose it was.

qa.q: What did Sahil think each night as he walked past the sink in week two?
qa.a: He thought his one pot was nothing compared with all the other mess, so it did not seem to matter.

qa.q: What choice could Sahil make after reading Dolma's list?
qa.a: He could wash all his items that night and suggest the house agree on who cleans when, since the list shows his small bits added up to a quarter of the mess.

qa.q: How might the list look to the other housemates when they read it?
qa.a: Each of them might be surprised, like Sahil, to see their own small items adding up, and might feel embarrassed to find their name on so many lines.

grounding: In a shared student kitchen each housemate leaves a little mess assuming it is too small to matter, until the pile makes the kitchen unusable for everyone.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: I'm Tenzin, and I share a co-living flat in Hyderabad with three others. This is what I saw this week, and I was part of it. On Monday Nirmala left the pressure cooker in the sink. On Tuesday Arvind left rice in a pan on the stove. I left my tiffin boxes on the counter, because honestly, what are two boxes? By Thursday the sink was blocked and the fridge smelled of old milk. Nobody said anything; we just ate out. Saturday was Nirmala's birthday. She had planned to cook biryani for all of us. She opened the kitchen door, stood there a long time, and closed it again. I can't say what she was thinking. She ordered food instead. I washed my two boxes that night, though it hardly touched the pile.

qa.q: What had Nirmala planned to cook on her birthday?
qa.a: She had planned to cook biryani for all of them.

qa.q: What did Tenzin believe about the tiffin boxes left on the counter?
qa.a: Tenzin believed two boxes were too small to matter, thinking 'what are two boxes?' when the others were leaving things too.

qa.q: What could the flatmates have done at the point where the sink was blocked and nobody spoke up?
qa.a: Someone could have called a short flat meeting and agreed who cleans on which day, instead of everyone eating out and waiting.

qa.q: How is Nirmala affected by the state of the kitchen on her birthday?
qa.a: She loses the birthday meal she planned to cook for everyone, and standing silently at the door suggests she is disappointed, though Tenzin cannot be sure what she thought.

grounding: Flatmates, including the narrator, each leave a little mess in the shared kitchen thinking it cannot matter, and the kitchen becomes unusable for everyone.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage: The co-working floor in Pune had two meeting rooms and forty people. By noon both were usually "booked" and empty, a bag on a chair, someone on a call in the corridor. Nilesh, twenty-five, a data analyst, had lost three client calls to it. At the Monday huddle he stood up with a printed page. "Two hours per booking at most. If nobody arrives within ten minutes, the room is free. Each week, two of us check the board at noon, by rota." Tarun, from the sales team, folded his arms. "And if people ignore it?" "Two no-shows and you can't book for a week. Me included." That afternoon Nilesh cancelled his own all-day booking for Thursday and split it into one short slot. People noticed.

qa.q: How long could a single booking last under Nilesh's plan?
qa.a: A booking could last two hours at most.

qa.q: Why does Tarun fold his arms when Nilesh presents the plan?
qa.a: Tarun doubts people will follow it and is waiting to see whether the rules have any teeth.

qa.q: Which choice by Nilesh made his rules more believable, and why?
qa.a: Cancelling his own all-day Thursday booking and taking one short slot showed he would follow the rules first, so people could trust that they were fair.

qa.q: What would change for Tarun's sales team if the rules hold?
qa.a: They would find a room free when they actually need one, instead of losing calls to rooms held by an empty bag on a chair.

grounding: A young analyst proposes booking limits, a shared check rota and a consequence for a common meeting room, and follows the rule himself first.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage:
Subject: Visitor parking, a proposal

Dear Sarita Didi,

As secretary of our residents' association, you've heard the complaints. Our six visitor spots are full of our own second cars and scooters, some for weeks. My parents couldn't park on Sunday and had to leave the car two lanes away.

Here's what I'd like to put to Saturday's meeting:
1. Visitor spots are for visitors only, up to one day.
2. Any flat can book a spot for a longer stay on a sheet at the gate.
3. Two volunteers a week check the spots, by rota. Anyone can see the sheet.
4. Break it twice and you lose booking for a month.

I moved my own spare scooter out of spot 4 this morning, so it starts with me.

Warm regards,
Vijay (Flat 12)

qa.q: Where did Vijay's parents have to leave their car on Sunday?
qa.a: They had to leave the car two lanes away.

qa.q: What does Vijay hope the association will feel about his proposal?
qa.a: Vijay hopes they will see it as fair to everyone, which is why the sheet is open to anyone and the rule applies to Flat 12 as well.

qa.q: Which part of Vijay's plan is most likely to build trust, and why?
qa.a: Moving his own spare scooter out of spot 4 before the meeting shows Vijay is not asking others to do anything Vijay won't do, which makes the rules easier to accept.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the email as secretary?
qa.a: Sarita may be relieved to receive a concrete plan instead of another complaint, and one she can put to the meeting with an example already set.

grounding: A young resident proposes clear limits, rota-based monitoring and consequences for shared parking, and applies the rule to their own spare scooter first.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Share or cheat in a game [Actor]
passage: I'm Saurabh. When I was eleven, my friend Chetan and I played a big board game about building cities. At the start we shook hands: "We never attack each other. Only the computer players." For three evenings it worked, and we were both winning. Then my city got rich. I kept looking at Chetan's army next to my border. What if he attacks tonight? I'll lose everything and look stupid for trusting him. So I attacked first. Chetan just stared. "I wasn't going to," he said. After that we attacked each other every single game, and the computer players won. We stopped playing that game. I still think about how scared I was of being the one who got tricked.

qa.q: What did Saurabh and Chetan promise each other at the start?
qa.a: They promised never to attack each other, only the computer players.

qa.q: What was Saurabh afraid of just before attacking?
qa.a: Saurabh was afraid Chetan would attack first and Saurabh would lose everything and look stupid for trusting him.

qa.q: What could Saurabh have done instead of attacking, once the fear set in?
qa.a: Saurabh could have told Chetan about the worry over the army at his border and asked him to move it, keeping the promise instead of breaking it first.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel when Saurabh attacks, and how does it change their games?
qa.a: He is shocked and hurt because he had no plan to attack, and after that he stops trusting Saurabh, so they fight each other every game and the computer players win.

grounding: A child breaks a fair pact in a game out of fear that the friend will cheat first, and both end up worse off.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Share or cheat in a game [Actor]
passage:
Summer camp note, Day 4. Written by Rajni, activity counsellor.

Today's game was Market Day: pairs agree to swap beads fairly, and both win a sticker if the counts match. Vishal, nine, and Kunal agreed to swap ten beads each. When they opened their hands, Kunal had ten. Vishal had six, and four more in his sock. When I asked him quietly, Vishal said, "I thought Kunal would keep some back. I didn't want to be the only one who gave all his." His ears were red. I told him that feeling is very common. Then I asked what he thought would happen if both boys hid beads. He thought, and said, "Nobody gets the sticker." He gave Kunal the four beads and asked to play the round again.

qa.q: How many beads did Vishal have in his sock?
qa.a: He had four more beads in his sock.

qa.q: What was Vishal worried about when he hid the beads?
qa.a: He was worried Kunal would keep some back and he would be the only one who gave all his beads.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Vishal in the conversation with Rajni?
qa.a: When Rajni asked what would happen if both boys hid beads, he worked out that nobody would get the sticker, and he chose to give the beads back and replay the round.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when he sees Vishal had hidden beads?
qa.a: Kunal might feel let down, since he gave all ten honestly, and he might be careful about trusting Vishal next time.

grounding: A nine-year-old cheats in a trading game because he fears his partner will cheat first, and a counsellor helps him see that both lose if both cheat.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: I'm Parveen. In Class 11, Gurleen and I were paired to present a working water-filter model at the school exhibition. We were both good students, which was the problem. I thought, Gurleen loves building things, she'll make it. I'll prepare the speech on the night before. Gurleen, I found out later, thought, Parveen is so organised, she'll make sure it's done. Each of us made the choice that seemed smartest for ourselves. Two days before, we finally met with a bucket of sand, a cut bottle and no plan. The model leaked in front of the judges, onto the principal's shoes. We got a participation certificate. What stung was knowing that if we'd both worked, even half as hard as usual, we would have done well.

qa.q: What happened to the water-filter model in front of the judges?
qa.a: It leaked, onto the principal's shoes.

qa.q: What did Parveen think about Gurleen before the exhibition?
qa.a: She thought Gurleen loves building things and would make the model, so Parveen could leave her own part until the night before.

qa.q: What choice would have changed the result for both girls?
qa.a: If each had done her own agreed part early instead of counting on the other, even half-hearted work together would have beaten the leaking model.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when she learns what Parveen had been thinking?
qa.a: She might feel a little annoyed but also recognise herself, since she had made the same bet about Parveen.

grounding: Two teenage girls each shirk their joint exhibition work expecting the other to cover, and both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Debate coach's note, Friday. Written by Kishore Sir.

Ujjwal and Hemlata, both Class 12, were partners in today's inter-house debate. Last week they agreed Ujjwal would prepare rebuttals and Hemlata the opening. Today the opening was thin and there were no rebuttals at all. They lost to the house that came fourth last year.

Afterwards I spoke to each alone. Ujjwal said, "She always over-prepares, Sir. I thought she'd cover the rebuttals too." Hemlata said, "He's good at thinking on his feet. I thought he'd carry it if I did less." Both looked miserable, and a little angry with each other.

My next step: on Monday I'll sit them down together, show them both answers side by side, and have them write their parts on one sheet with dates.

qa.q: Which parts had Ujjwal and Hemlata agreed to prepare?
qa.a: Ujjwal would prepare the rebuttals and Hemlata the opening.

qa.q: What did each partner think about the other before the debate?
qa.a: Ujjwal assumed Hemlata would over-prepare and cover his part, and Hemlata assumed Ujjwal would carry the debate on his feet if she did less.

qa.q: Why is showing them both answers side by side a useful next step?
qa.a: Seeing that each made the same bet would help them understand that both shirking made both lose, and writing parts with dates makes each accountable.

qa.q: How does the loss look to the rival house that won?
qa.a: They may be pleasantly surprised to beat a strong pair, not knowing the pair lost because each left the work to the other.

grounding: Two teenage debate partners each do less expecting the other to cover, so both lose, as recorded by their coach.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Mentor's note, 12 March. Written by Mrs Fernandes, first-year mentor.

Shreya, nineteen, came to see me today, shaking. All term she has shared her physiology notes with the whole study group, including Nazia, who always said she'd send hers "after the test" and never did. Today the internal results came out. Nazia ranked second, Shreya eleventh, and a classmate told Shreya that Nazia's answers were almost her notes word for word. Shreya said, "I feel like such a fool. I'm never giving anyone anything again." She has already refused two new first-years who asked to study with her.

I listened, and I told her the anger made sense. I also asked her to think about whether those first-years had done anything to her. We will meet again next week to talk about sharing with people who give back.

qa.q: What rank did Shreya get in the internal results?
qa.a: Shreya ranked eleventh.

qa.q: What is Shreya feeling after the results come out, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She feels foolish and angry, since she arrives shaking, calls herself a fool and says she will never give anyone anything again.

qa.q: What choice is in front of Shreya now, and what might help her make it?
qa.a: She can shut everyone out or share with people who give back; trying a small swap with one of the first-years would let her test trust without being used again.

qa.q: How might the two first-years see Shreya's refusal?
qa.a: They may feel confused or rejected, because they did nothing wrong and are paying for what Nazia did.

grounding: A student who shared notes freely is used by a peer who never reciprocated, feels foolish and angry, and starts refusing everyone.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Tuesday night

Mock test rankings came out at the coaching centre today. Uday: 14th. Me: 37th.

For two months I've given Uday my formula sheets, my solved papers, even the shortcut tricks I worked out myself. Every time he said, "Next week I'll send you my chemistry notes, Pallavi." Next week never came. Today I heard him tell the others he "figured out" the shortcuts on his own.

I came back to my PG room and just sat on the bed. I feel so stupid. Like everyone could see I was being used except me.

And then Sunanda from the next room knocked and asked if we could revise organic together. I said I was busy. She looked surprised. I'm not busy. I just don't want to be the fool again.

But Sunanda has never taken anything from me. Why did I punish her?

qa.q: What rank did Uday get in the mock test?
qa.a: Uday ranked 14th.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling while sitting on the bed after coming back?
qa.a: Pallavi felt stupid and hurt, as if everyone else could see the using that Pallavi had missed.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try with Sunanda tomorrow?
qa.a: Pallavi could offer to revise one chapter of organic together and see if Sunanda shares back, instead of shutting out someone who has never taken advantage of Pallavi.

qa.q: How might Sunanda have seen Pallavi's answer at the door?
qa.a: Sunanda may have felt surprised and brushed off, not knowing that Pallavi's refusal was really about Uday.

grounding: A student whose shared notes were used by a peer who never reciprocated feels foolish and angry and starts refusing others, then questions it.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: Salma and Elizabeth had run neighbouring counters at a food court in Kolkata since they were eighteen, Salma at the rolls stall, Elizabeth at the juice bar. Four years of small deals: Elizabeth watched the rolls when Salma went for prayers; Salma kept Elizabeth's cash box when she ran to the bank. Each favour was always returned. Then, one busy Saturday, a man asked Elizabeth where he could order food for a birthday party of sixty. Salma was on her break. Elizabeth could easily have said, "Try the stall at the other end." She remembered Rinku, who used to run the momo counter. He had once taken a big order that was meant for Salma, and after that nobody on the floor would cover for him. When Salma came back, Elizabeth handed her the man's number.

qa.q: What did Salma do for Elizabeth when she ran to the bank?
qa.a: Salma kept Elizabeth's cash box.

qa.q: What was on Elizabeth's mind when she thought of Rinku?
qa.a: She was remembering how one grab at Salma's order left Rinku without anyone to cover for him, and she did not want to lose Salma's trust the same way.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Elizabeth, and why?
qa.a: Passing the party order to Salma kept four years of trust intact, which is worth more to her in the long run than one order, since they will work side by side for years.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when Elizabeth hands her the number?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel grateful and more sure of being able to count on Elizabeth, making her even more willing to return the favour.

grounding: Two young colleagues who have traded favours for years keep cooperating because they will keep meeting, while a past betrayal by another stall-holder is remembered.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: "Bhupen, you look like you've seen a ghost." Alka set down two cups of tea in the lab's back room. "The sample labels for batch 7. They're swapped. I did them last night." "Swapped? Sir will go mad." "He thinks you did the labels. Your initials are on the tray." Alka stared at him, her cup halfway to her mouth. "And?" "And I could just... let him think that." Silence. "You could," Alka said slowly. "And I'd find out. And then what?" Bhupen rubbed his face. "Then you'd never cover my night shift again." "Two years we've swapped shifts. Remember when I covered your sister's wedding?" "I remember." He stood up. "I'll tell him it was me." "I'll come with you," Alka said. "We'll fix the tray together."

qa.q: Whose initials were on the tray of batch 7?
qa.a: Alka's initials were on the tray.

qa.q: What was Bhupen worried about when he admitted the mistake to Alka?
qa.a: He was worried about the supervisor's anger, and then about losing Alka's trust and her help with his night shifts if he let her take the blame.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation?
qa.a: When Alka asked 'And then what?', Bhupen saw that blaming her would end two years of swapped shifts, so he chose to own the mistake.

qa.q: How does Alka see Bhupen's choice to tell the truth?
qa.a: Alka sees it as the kind of reliability that matters between them, so Alka offers to go with him and fix the tray together.

grounding: Two young lab colleagues who have cooperated for years show that, because they will keep working together, keeping faith is both practical and right.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Thursday, 11 pm

Today Afreen covered my site visit in Thane without being asked, because I had fever. Writing it down so I remember how we got here.

When I joined in June, I shared my checklists with her on day one, no conditions. She shared her drawings back. Good start.

Then in August she skipped her two agreed site visits and I did them. I didn't sulk or skip mine to get even. I just said, "Afreen, I did your visits twice. That's not our deal. I need you to do yours." She went quiet, then said, "You're right. It was a bad month. It won't happen again." It didn't.

So I let it go completely. No keeping score.

And now she's the one standing on a muddy site at eight in the morning for me. Glad I didn't give up on her in August.
- Zubin

qa.q: Why did Afreen cover Zubin's site visit today?
qa.a: Because Zubin had fever.
